source.title: Multiple Descent: Design Your Own Generalization Curve
source.authors: Lin Chen; Yi-Fei Min; Mikhail Belkin; Amin Karbasi

record.tranche_reason: The paper proves that linear-regression generalization curves can have arbitrarily many controlled rises and falls, refining the claim that double descent is a general, characteristic curve.
record.gate_note: The paper's own results are theoretical constructions for linear regression, not deep-network experiments. Results cited in related work, including epoch-wise and sample-wise findings, are not rows. The underparameterized monotonicity result is not recorded as a row because it does not measure the post-interpolation behavior named by V4.
record.test_reason: The paper proves that the overparameterized linear-regression risk curve can be made to rise or fall at any chosen dimension. The authors argue this shows double descent is not intrinsic to a model family. That is a specific argument that the general double-descent curve (V4) needs restating. It also proves that multiple peaks can exist (part of V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors prove that linear-regression risk can show multiple descents with controllable ascents and descents away from the interpolation threshold. They conclude that U-shaped and double-descent curves are not intrinsic to the model family but come from interactions between data properties and the algorithm's inductive bias. They also note that complex curves are rarely seen in practice outside curated constructions.
record.recipe_differences: The paper gives theoretical constructions for least-squares linear regression using a feature-revealing process and chosen Gaussian or Gaussian-mixture feature distributions; it does not reproduce deep-network size or epoch sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The shape depends on the distributions and order of the revealed features; Gaussian features can produce descents and Gaussian-mixture features can produce ascents.
record.problems: The evidence is theoretical and relies on carefully constructed feature distributions; it does not empirically validate the behavior in deep networks or typical practical settings. The overparameterized construction has the stated technical starting condition d ≥ n + 8.
record.rows_left_out: Theorem 1's non-decreasing underparameterized risk and Theorem 4's arbitrarily large underparameterized increase are outside the post-interpolation behavior in V4. Intermediate lemmas and theorems establishing the overparameterized constructions were not duplicated as rows.

untested.parts: Varying sample size; n is fixed throughout.
Model classes other than min-norm linear regression; behaviour at the interpolation threshold itself (results start at d ≥ n+8).
No effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
Whether label noise drives peaks; whether optimal regularization removes them. The analysis is unregularized least squares.

missing.what: Theorem 1: in the underparameterized regime (d<n), risk is non-decreasing for any data distribution, so no classical U-shape occurs before interpolation. This bears on V4's claim to subsume the U-shaped curve.
Theorem 4: adding a Gaussian-mixture feature can raise underparameterized risk by any amount. Feature order alone changes the curve for the same data.

record.verdict_notes: Belkin is a coauthor, but this paper is not an original source, so verdicts are given. The evidence is purely theoretical existence results. The constructions start at d ≥ n+8 and are unregularized. In the β=0 case the loss is the variance term only. The record's rows_left_out excludes Theorem 1, but that result is relevant to V4's U-shape subsumption, so it is listed under missing.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size sweeps and the peak near the training-set interpolation size.
Changing sample size near an interpolation threshold; sample size is fixed in the main analysis.
The paper studies constructed linear-regression settings, not whether the same curve occurs across model classes generally or in deep networks.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
The paper does not test whether label noise or variance drives peaks, whether optimally tuned regularization removes them, or whether those factors produce multiple peaks.
No alternative effective-parameter count is used to assess whether a second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: linear regression, β = 0, minimum-norm solution
rows.size_stated: data dimension d; n + 8 ≤ d ≤ D − 1
rows.operation_detail: Increase the number of revealed features; choose each new feature distribution to prescribe an ascent or descent.

conditions.value: product distribution; first n + 8 features are N(0, 1), later features are Gaussian or Gaussian mixtures

rows.measure: Expected excess generalization loss Ld as feature dimension increases
rows.value: For any prescribed sequence, Ld+1 > Ld when Δd = ↑ and Ld+1 < Ld when Δd = ↓.
rows.note: Existence result: the feature distributions are constructed to obtain the specified sequence, so this is not evidence that arbitrary practical model families exhibit the curve.
rows.check: Theorem 5 shows any prescribed rise/fall sequence past interpolation, so a second descent can occur but is not guaranteed. For V6's multiple-peak part the result is observed; label noise and regularization are not varied.

source_check.correct: V4: partial, because post-interpolation improvement depends on the constructed feature distributions. V6 multiple-peak component: observed, because arbitrary rise/fall sequences permit arbitrarily many local maxima. Regularization dependence is untested.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5, Theorem 5 and its proof; Section 3, definition of multiple descent.
source_check.problem: The single partial state does not fit the fully established multiple-peak component of V6.

rows.subject: linear regression, β = 0, minimum-norm solution
rows.operation_detail: Add a Gaussian feature with a chosen variance.

conditions.value: a1, b1, …, bn ∼ N(0, σ²), with σ chosen by the theorem
E[‖(AᵀA)+x‖²] > 0 and the finite-expectation conditions in equation (4)

rows.measure: Expected excess generalization loss change Ld+1 − Ld
rows.value: There exists σ > 0 such that Ld+1 − Ld < 0.
rows.note: A constructed descent as one more feature is revealed.
rows.check: Theorem 8: adding a Gaussian feature with suitable variance lowers risk past interpolation. This is consistent with V4's further descent.

rows.subject: linear regression, β = 0, minimum-norm solution
rows.operation_detail: Add a Gaussian-mixture feature with chosen parameters.

conditions.value: a1, b1, …, bn ∼ Nσ,μmix, with σ and μ chosen by the theorem

rows.measure: Expected excess generalization loss change Ld+1 − Ld
rows.value: For any C > 0, there exist μ and σ such that Ld+1 − Ld > C.
rows.note: The theorem permits an arbitrarily large increase by constructing the feature distribution.
rows.check: Theorem 9: adding a Gaussian-mixture feature can raise risk by any amount C past interpolation. This is the opposite of 'risk improves again'.

rows.subject: linear regression with β ∼ N(0, ρ²), expected risk, minimum-norm solution
rows.size_stated: data dimension d; n + 8 ≤ d ≤ D − 1
rows.operation_detail: Increase the number of revealed features and choose each new feature distribution to prescribe an ascent or descent.

conditions.value: product distribution; first n + 8 features are N(0, 1), later features are Gaussian or Gaussian mixtures

rows.measure: Expected risk Ldexp as feature dimension increases
rows.value: For any prescribed sequence, Ld+1exp > Ldexp when Δd = ↑ and Ld+1exp < Ldexp when Δd = ↓.
rows.note: Existence result for Gaussian-distributed β; the theorem constructs the feature distributions and, for descents, chooses a suitable ρ.
rows.check: Theorem 11 is the same arbitrary-sequence result for Gaussian β with risk averaged over β; ρ must be small enough. For V6's multiple-peak part the result is observed.

source_check.correct: V4: partial, because post-interpolation improvement depends on the constructed feature distributions. V6 multiple-peak component: observed. Theorem 11 establishes existence of a suitable positive rho and product feature distribution for any prescribed rise/fall sequence; the proof bounds rho at descent steps. Regularization dependence is untested.

relation.reason: The study proves its own results about post-interpolation risk changes and multiple descent.

tranche.reason: The constructed risk curves and the explicit argument that double descent is not intrinsic to a model family qualify the general V4 claim.

source_check.notes: These are existence constructions away from interpolation, not empirical prevalence results. For beta = 0 the response-noise variance is normalized to one; Gaussian-beta descents require suitably small rho relative to the noise scale.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The results establish that increasing feature dimension can produce descents, including within arbitrarily specified rise-fall sequences (r1–r4).

reader_labels.reason: The results show that the curve can be made to rise or fall at chosen steps, so a standard double-descent shape is not intrinsic to these model families (r1, r4).
